raw_response:
I am 67 years old, and I have farmed this land in Quzhou since I was a young girl. I never went to school, but I know my fields. At my age, I do not have the strength or the desire to try new things. I do what has always worked.

My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October after rotary tilling the land. I keep about 5 mu for the wheat-maize rotation. That is enough for me to handle. I use the improved wheat seed that I save from last year or get from my neighbors — varieties like the local shimai or lumai types that everyone grows. Wheat gives me flour for my own steamed bread and noodles, and I sell what is left. For the wheat, I will irrigate four times: once more before the winter ends, and then at green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, and I will topdress with some urea or ammonium bicarbonate when the wheat starts growing again in spring. I spray for weeds and insects two or three times — when the shopkeeper tells me it is time, or when I see the neighbors spraying.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant maize the same day. Everyone here plants hybrid maize — Denghai or Nongda seeds that I buy from the agricultural shop. You cannot save hybrid seed; it will not grow right. I do not till for the maize — I plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time and labor before the summer rains. I give the maize one bag of compound fertilizer at planting, irrigate twice during the summer if it does not rain enough, and spray two or three times for insects and weeds. By October, I harvest the maize, sell most of it, and keep some to feed the chickens.

I do not grow cotton anymore — my back cannot take the bending and pruning. I do not grow vegetables for the market because the prices change too much and I do not have the energy to haul them to town. Wheat and maize are safe. The state buys them, and I know I will not go hungry.
